newsitem.title: UK: North Sea crude sellers cash in on Iraqi delays.
newsitem.headline: North Sea crude sellers cash in on Iraqi delays.

text.p: The North Sea crude market held firm on Wednesday as sellers took advantage of the continued absence of Iraqi crude to push up premiums.

The Aug/Sep Brent intermonth spread traded higher at +15 cents, having changed hands at a high of +14 cents on Tuesday and +15.5 cents in the U.S. aftermarket. Sep/Oct gained a few cents to trade at -4 cents.
Outright levels were also slightly stronger, with September Brent five cents up at $18.27 a barrel at 1110 GMT.
"People have been holding back waiting for Iraqi oil but they can't wait that long," said one trader.
"I think there's some hidden buying waiting to get done which should run the differentials up."
The U.N. said on Tuesday that approval of an Iraqi aid plan, which Iraq insists on before it will resume exports, was not expected before the end of July.
Traders expect that agreeing new price formulae and signing new contracts will take a further two weeks, and see mid-August as the earliest start-date for sales.
Brent, Ekofisk, Forties and Oseberg all traded at strong differentials on Tuesday.

Traders speculated that a French refiner which bought at least three Brent cargoes, two at a five cent premium to recent levels, had shorts to a U.S. refiner which has chartered a VLCC for a transatlantic trip in early August.
A single Brent cargo, loading August 7-9 was due to turn wet on Wednesday.
North Sea production problems were also lending support to the market, with the Nelson field in the Forties system and Snorre which feeds the Statfjord stream both out of action.
The Nelson field, which was already running below capacity, was shut down completely on Tuesday night at least until Friday.
That was due to a fault in a water system pipe, operator Enterprise said.
Enterprise had already planned to cut output at the 150,000 barrel per day (bpd) field to below 50,000 bpd at the end of the week to allow repairs to a gas dehydration system.
Norway's Saga Petroleum said the 200,000 bpd Snorre field which was shut in on Sunday due to a power fault would be down until Friday.

Norwegian traders said that a decision would be made this afternoon on any changes to the Statfjord loading programme. Statfjord has been one of the weaker grades recently, with sales of August cargoes getting off to a slow start.
